read: full: abstract, sections I-IV (introduction, related work, construction, evaluation protocol), V-VI (experiments, analysis), VIII-X (discussion, limitations, conclusion) and Appendix C-F (p.1-25); section VII (fine-tuning, RAG and prompting interventions, p.15-20) skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2604.17966v1 [cs.AI], 20 April 2026 (p.1 margin stamp); no venue shown.
what_it_is: A static benchmark of closed-form calculation problems in hypersonic aerodynamics and high-temperature gas dynamics (thermal protection system engineering), all derived from Anderson's Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics (2nd ed.), apparently from its Chinese translation (p.4, p.22). A human-AI pipeline (automatic extraction, rule and LLM checks, domain-expert review, a triple-reviewer go/no-go gate) reduced 4,560 raw candidates to a 420-item core set over four difficulty levels and eight domains, keeping an 810-item pre-gating set as a noise control (p.1, p.4-7). Scoring has two tracks: relative-error bands on the final numeric answer with a unit check, and an 8-dimension reasoning rubric (formula selection to presentation) scored 0-2 by a Gemini-3-Pro-Preview judge given the reference solution, calibrated against one domain expert on 62 items (p.7-10). It reports that 9.5% to 14.3% of items per model are 'right answer, wrong reasoning' (Table XXII, p.20-21).
domain: engineering: aerospace (hypersonic thermal protection systems; Newtonian theory, shock relations, boundary layers, aerothermal heating, viscous interaction, chemical equilibrium, nonequilibrium flow, radiation)
size: 420 core items (L1 170, L2 120, L3 80, L4 50) plus an 810-item pre-gating set, from 4,560 raw candidates (Table IV p.7, p.1). Models: 12 in the leaderboard tables (Tables VIII and X, p.12-13); the text says 13 models from 7 families (p.1, p.10) and names 6 more as excluded (p.10-11).
source_of_items: textbook: problems extracted from one graduate textbook (Anderson, 2nd ed.) by rule-based and LLM-assisted passes, then deduplicated, filtered and reviewed by domain experts, who also check the reference solution (p.4-6).
has_gold_traces: partial: each item has given parameters, named target quantities with units and weights (p.4-5) and an 'authoritative reference solution' that the judge receives (p.8), checked by experts in Stage 4 (p.6). No intermediate values are scored against gold.
evaluation: Two tracks, reported separately. Final answer: relative error banded Exact <1% (1.0), Acceptable 1-10% (0.7), Order-Correct 10-50% (0.3), Wrong (0); unit correctness as a separate binary; answers extracted by regex with an LLM fallback (p.7-9, Table V). Rubric by LLM judge: eight solution-level dimensions scored 0, 1 or 2 by Gemini-3-Pro-Preview against the reference solution, weighted into a 0-100 score (p.8-9, Table VI). The headline 'KPI' is the mean rubric score only (eq. 3, p.9-10), so the leaderboard is the judge's. Process quality is judged per dimension over the whole solution, not per step.
human_validation: Items: Stage 4 domain-expert review of 1,930 candidates for self-containedness, completeness, well-defined targets and correct reference solutions, rejecting 770; a triple-reviewer go/no-go gate on dataset readiness (p.6-7). The number of experts is not given. Evaluator: a 3-item pilot showed large judge leniency (p.25, Table XXIII). One domain expert then scored 62 items on all 8 dimensions: weighted Cohen's kappa 0.68 to 0.82 per dimension (overall 0.75), with the judge lenient on calculation accuracy (+0.08) and physical plausibility (+0.11). Spearman 0.94 between human and judge rankings of 6 models, and the 7 items (11%) differing by 2 or more points were adjudicated by a third reviewer (p.8-10, Table VII).
contamination_measures: none against pretraining contamination: the items come from a published textbook (p.4). A chapter-grouped train/dev/test split prevents leakage into the paper's own fine-tuning experiments (p.6-7). The paper notes performance tracks 'the density of relevant training data' (p.15).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it. It contradicts the May claim that engineering benchmarks 'remain limited to outcome matching': it scores reasoning quality separately from the answer and measures 'right answer, wrong reasoning' (p.8-10, p.20-21).

suggested_wording: TPS-CalcBench (Zheng et al., 2026) scores 420 textbook calculation problems in hypersonic thermal-protection engineering on two separate tracks, answer accuracy and an eight-dimension reasoning rubric graded by an LLM judge calibrated against one domain expert (weighted kappa 0.68 to 0.82), and finds 'right answer, wrong reasoning' on roughly a tenth of items.
facts_to_cite: 420 core items from 4,560 candidates extracted from one graduate textbook (Anderson, Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics), over four difficulty levels and eight domains (p.1, p.4, Table IV p.7)
Construction combines automatic extraction and filtering with domain-expert review and a triple-reviewer go/no-go gate (p.5-7)
Outcome track: relative-error bands (<1%, 1-10%, 10-50%, 50% or more) and a separate unit check (p.7-9, Table V)

Process track: eight rubric dimensions (formula selection, parameter identification, unit consistency, calculation accuracy, physical plausibility, assumption justification, result interpretation, presentation) scored 0-2 by a Gemini-3-Pro-Preview judge given the reference solution (p.8-9, Table VI)
Judge-expert agreement on 62 items: weighted kappa 0.68 to 0.82 per dimension, overall 0.75; the judge is more lenient on calculation accuracy and physical plausibility (p.9-10, Table VII)
Outcome-high but process-low ('right answer, wrong reasoning') on 9.5% to 14.3% of scored items per model (Table XXII, p.20-21)
Rankings shift between the 810-item pre-gating set and the 420-item core set (p.11, p.15, Table XIII)
Items are static and textbook-derived, with no measure against pretraining contamination (p.4, p.6-7)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering calculation problems (adjacent to EngTrace's thermodynamics, transport and fluid domains, though in aerospace, outside the five branches); difficulty tiers (p.7); separate outcome and process scores, and the 'right answer, wrong reasoning' concern, which parallels EngTrace's finding that 93 of 228 correct-answer traces contain an incorrect step; a relative-error answer check with a unit check (p.7-9); calibration of the judge against expert ratings (p.8-10). Lacks: generated instances (static textbook items, contamination unaddressed); gold intermediate values (the judge gets a reference solution, p.8); deterministic step checks (process quality is an LLM rubric score); step-level verdicts (the rubric dimensions cover the whole solution); multi-branch scope; a private test set. Its expert calibration is one expert on 62 items. What EngTrace adds beyond it: code-computed milestones and per-claim arithmetic checked deterministically at each step, generated instances from a private seed across five branches, and a residual judge validated against independent step labels from 15 experts.
notes: (1) Model-count inconsistency: '13 models from 7 families' (p.1, p.10), but Tables VIII and X list 12 models, the text speaks of '12 ranked models' (p.11) and names 6 excluded models (p.10-11), 18 in all. (2) The 'composite KPI' is the mean LLM-judge rubric score (eq. 3, p.9-10); the Table X caption says it combines outcome 'via G4', but G4 is the judge's arithmetic rating, not Track 1. Cite Track 1 and the rubric separately, not the KPI as a combined measure. (3) The fine-tuning base model is given only as 'aws.claude-sonnet-4.5 or deepseek-v3.1' (p.17), so the intervention gains are hard to interpret; they are irrelevant to EngTrace anyway. (4) The items appear to be in Chinese, from the textbook's Chinese translation (p.22). (5) The web search note's description ('one domain expert audited 62 items', kappa 0.68 to 0.82, lenient on calculation accuracy and plausibility) matches the text.
